support.title: Diarrhoea and fluids
support.text: Keep the prescribed anti-diarrhoea plan available from the first dose. Report loose stools early and keep drinking if able. Persistent or severe diarrhoea, weakness, inability to drink or much less urine requires urgent advice. The team decides whether to hold treatment and when it is safe to restart.

support.title: Skin, nails and mouth
support.text: Use the agreed skin, nail and mouth-care plan. Report rash, painful nails or mouth sores early. Emollients and sun protection may help; the team decides whether creams, antibiotics or other treatment are needed. Blistering or peeling skin needs urgent assessment.

support.title: Nausea medicines
support.text: Erlotinib has minimal-to-low oral emetic risk. Agree any as-needed anti-sickness medicine with the team. Routine infusion premedication is not required.

support.title: Medicine interactions
support.text: Give pharmacy all medicines and supplements. Strong CYP3A4 inducers or inhibitors, grapefruit and medicines for stomach acid can change exposure. Avoid proton pump inhibitor combinations unless the specialist resolves the plan. Necessary antacids require source-specific separation; ask for written timing. Warfarin needs extra blood-clotting checks. Smoking reduces exposure; get cessation support and do not change your cancer dose yourself.

support.title: Pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding
support.text: Avoid pregnancy. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after the final dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for at least 2 weeks after the final dose. Discuss fertility and future pregnancy plans before starting.

support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding requires a specialist decision; contact your team promptly if pregnancy occurs.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: Adjuvant: maximum 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance: until progression or unacceptable toxicity. ES-SCLC requires completed induction; this suite contains no induction chemotherapy.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between treatment visits.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

sections.title: Appointments
sections.text: Atezolizumab 1200 mg is given by intravenous infusion on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The first infusion lasts about 60 minutes; later infusions may last 30 minutes if tolerated. The visit includes checks and preparation. This protocol also offers a separately prescribed 1875 mg injection under the skin of the thigh over about 7 minutes every 3 weeks. The IV and under-skin doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

sections.title: Course length
sections.text: Adjuvant treatment lasts up to 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance continue until progression or unacceptable toxicity, with regular individual review.

sections.title: Checks between visits
sections.text: Blood tests are due before each infusion. Thyroid tests stay every 3–6 weeks regardless of dose schedule. Ask about travel, work, transport and whom to contact if a test or visit is delayed.

sections.title: Home medicines and records
sections.text: Keep the alert card, symptom record, current medicine list and urgent contact details accessible. Your team may prescribe steroids or hormone replacement only if needed.

sections.title: After the final dose
sections.text: Keep reporting new symptoms. Some hormone medicines and monitoring continue after the cancer treatment finishes.

chapters.title: How atezolizumab works
chapters.intro: This is an immunotherapy medicine.

items.title: PD-L1 blockade
items.text: Atezolizumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can help cancer cells evade immune attack. Blocking PD-L1 can help immune cells attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.

items.title: Healthy organs can be affected
items.text: Immune inflammation can affect lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin, glands, muscles, heart and nerves. It may need steroids, hospital care or long-term hormone replacement, and can start after treatment ends.

items.text: Confirm diagnosis, treatment setting and relevant biomarkers. Blood count, kidney/liver profile, glucose, thyroid and hepatitis screening provide a baseline. Discuss existing illness and all medicines.

items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 3-week treatment cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks; other hormones when clinically indicated. Symptoms need review during and after treatment.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

chapters.intro: Use the contact plan given by your oncology service.

items.title: Report warning symptoms
items.text: Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

items.title: During the drip
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately if you become itchy, flushed, breathless, dizzy, tight-chested or suddenly unwell.

items.title: Care after treatment ends
items.text: Immune inflammation can start late. Tell any healthcare team about atezolizumab even after the course has finished.

factors: First-line metastatic NSCLC requires PD-L1 ≥50% tumour cells or ≥10% immune cells and no EGFR/ALK alteration. After prior chemotherapy, NSCLC has separate eligibility. Adjuvant use requires completely resected high-risk stage II–IIIA AJCC7, predominantly non-squamous cancer, PD-L1 ≥50%, no EGFR/ALK alteration and prior platinum chemotherapy. ECOG 0–1. Adjuvant platinum must commence within 12 weeks of surgery and atezolizumab within 12 weeks of the last platinum dose; no progression after chemotherapy.

First-line metastatic: no previous systemic treatment for stage IV disease; previous perioperative chemotherapy requires treatment-free interval ≥6 months. Post-chemotherapy NSCLC requires prior platinum and appropriate EGFR/ALK targeted treatment where relevant.

Symptomatic CNS metastases, hypersensitivity and clinically significant active infection are source exclusions. Symptomatic ILD and medical conditions requiring immunosuppression >10 mg/day prednisolone equivalent are source exclusions. Inhaled/topical steroids are excluded from that definition; autoimmune disease and previous checkpoint treatment require individual review.
alternatives: Consider setting-specific systemic therapy, targeted agents, clinical trials, surveillance and supportive care.
limitations: OAK, IMpower110, IMpower010 and IMpower133 used 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks. The 840 mg every 2 weeks, 1680 mg every 4 weeks and SC schedules rely on pharmacokinetic/formulation bridging, not separate head-to-head efficacy trials.
IMpower010 subgroup results are exploratory, unstratified PD-L1 ≥50%, EGFR/ALK-negative stage II–IIIA (n=209). Final DFS and second interim OS are not confirmatory overall-population OS results.
IMpower110 updated high-PD-L1 exploratory OS confidence interval crosses 1; distinguish it from the earlier positive primary analysis.
IMpower133 evaluates four-cycle combination induction followed by maintenance; it does not estimate the isolated benefit of maintenance alone.

Non-lung urothelial indications remain in the clinical protocol. This patient suite is lung-only; lung outcomes must not be used as urothelial evidence. Current access must be checked separately from trial evidence and licensing.

day_groups.title: Your infusion visit
day_groups.body: The team reviews your blood results, symptoms and medicines. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, a tight chest, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell during the drip.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

day_groups.title: Between visits
day_groups.body: You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment.
day_groups.action: Confirm thyroid checks every 3–6 weeks independently of infusion appointments.

support.title: Sickness medicines
support.text: Atezolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

support.title: Hormones and steroids
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding requires a specialist decision; contact your team promptly if pregnancy occurs.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: Adjuvant: maximum 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance: until progression or unacceptable toxicity. ES-SCLC requires completed induction; this suite contains no induction chemotherapy.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between treatment visits.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

evidence.intro: Atezolizumab may help the immune system control suitable lung cancers. After surgery and chemotherapy, it can reduce recurrence risk in a selected group. chapters.title: How atezolizumab works
chapters.intro: This is an immunotherapy medicine.

items.title: PD-L1 blockade
items.text: Atezolizumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can help cancer cells evade immune attack. Blocking PD-L1 can help immune cells attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.

items.title: Healthy organs can be affected
items.text: Immune inflammation can affect lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin, glands, muscles, heart and nerves. It may need steroids, hospital care or long-term hormone replacement, and can start after treatment ends.

chapters.intro: Keep your team informed about what matters to you.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use the contact plan given by your oncology service.

items.title: Report warning symptoms
items.text: Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

items.title: During the drip
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately if you become itchy, flushed, breathless, dizzy, tight-chested or suddenly unwell.

items.title: Care after treatment ends
items.text: Immune inflammation can start late. Tell any healthcare team about atezolizumab even after the course has finished.

factors: First-line metastatic NSCLC requires PD-L1 ≥50% tumour cells or ≥10% immune cells and no EGFR/ALK alteration. After prior chemotherapy, NSCLC has separate eligibility. Adjuvant use requires completely resected high-risk stage II–IIIA AJCC7, predominantly non-squamous cancer, PD-L1 ≥50%, no EGFR/ALK alteration and prior platinum chemotherapy. ECOG 0–1. Adjuvant platinum must commence within 12 weeks of surgery and atezolizumab within 12 weeks of the last platinum dose; no progression after chemotherapy.

Symptomatic CNS metastases, hypersensitivity and clinically significant active infection are source exclusions. Symptomatic ILD and immunosuppression >10 mg/day prednisolone equivalent are cautions in this source. alternatives: Consider setting-specific systemic therapy, targeted agents, clinical trials, surveillance and supportive care.
limitations: OAK, IMpower110, IMpower010 and IMpower133 used 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks. The 840 mg every 2 weeks, 1680 mg every 4 weeks and SC schedules rely on pharmacokinetic/formulation bridging, not separate head-to-head efficacy trials.

IMpower110 updated high-PD-L1 exploratory OS confidence interval crosses 1; distinguish it from the earlier positive primary analysis.
IMpower133 evaluates four-cycle combination induction followed by maintenance; it does not estimate the isolated benefit of maintenance alone.

day_groups.title: Your infusion visit
day_groups.body: The team reviews your blood results, symptoms and medicines. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, a tight chest, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell during the drip.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

day_groups.title: Between visits
day_groups.body: You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment.

support.title: Sickness medicines
support.text: Atezolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

support.title: Hormones and steroids
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding requires a specialist decision; contact your team promptly if pregnancy occurs.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: Adjuvant: maximum 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance: until progression or unacceptable toxicity. ES-SCLC requires completed induction; this suite contains no induction chemotherapy.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between treatment visits.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be offered
evidence.intro: Atezolizumab may help the immune system control suitable lung cancers. After surgery and chemotherapy, it can reduce recurrence risk in a selected group. evidence.interpretation: Separate lung settings and trials; group results are not personal predictions.

chapters.title: How atezolizumab works
chapters.intro: This is an immunotherapy medicine.

items.title: PD-L1 blockade
items.text: Atezolizumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can help cancer cells evade immune attack. Blocking PD-L1 can help immune cells attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.

items.title: Healthy organs can be affected
items.text: Immune inflammation can affect lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin, glands, muscles, heart and nerves. It may need steroids, hospital care or long-term hormone replacement, and can start after treatment ends.

items.title: After stopping

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

limitations: OAK, IMpower110, IMpower010 and IMpower133 used 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks. The 840 mg every 2 weeks, 1680 mg every 4 weeks and SC schedules rely on pharmacokinetic/formulation bridging, not separate head-to-head efficacy trials.

agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.
agents.watch: Report new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.

For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the aim for your exact lung setting, likely benefit, alternatives, important immune risks and how treatment may be paused or stopped. Some side effects need long-term medicines. Ask about fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and effects on daily life. For treatment after surgery, distinguish delaying recurrence from an overall-survival benefit, which was not established in the final trial analysis.
patient.safety_note: Immune effects can happen on any day and after treatment ends. Carry your immunotherapy alert card and tell any healthcare team that you receive pembrolizumab.

day_groups.title: Your infusion visit
day_groups.body: The team reviews your blood results, symptoms and medicines. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, a tight chest, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell during the drip.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

day_groups.title: Between visits
day_groups.body: You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment.
day_groups.action: Confirm thyroid tests are booked every 3–6 weeks, even if infusions are six weeks apart.

support.title: Sickness medicines
support.text: Pembrolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

support.title: Hormones and steroids
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least four months after the last dose. If pregnancy is possible or occurs, contact your oncology team promptly.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: The adjuvant course lasts up to 12 months. Metastatic treatment continues while helpful and tolerable; a 24-month review may lead to stopping or continuing. Symptoms, response and your preferences can change the plan.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between six-weekly infusions.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

questions.q: Does an abnormal blood test mean pembrolizumab must be stopped permanently?
questions.a: Not by itself. Your team checks whether the change is caused by immune inflammation, another medicine, cancer or another illness. They decide whether to pause treatment, investigate further or stop it. Do not change the treatment plan yourself.

patient.scope_note: This patient suite covers the two lung indications described here. The shared clinical protocol also lists other cancers, which need their own patient information.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be offered
evidence.intro: In a trial of suitable people with metastatic lung cancer and a high PD-L1 result, pembrolizumab helped people live longer than chemotherapy. After surgery and chemotherapy, a separate trial found a lower risk of recurrence or death. Its final long-term analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in overall survival. The aims and evidence differ between these settings.
evidence.interpretation: These results describe groups of people, not what will happen to one person. The metastatic and after-surgery studies answer different questions.
evidence.population: Two separate lung settings: untreated metastatic PD-L1-high NSCLC; and resected NSCLC at high recurrence risk after chemotherapy.
evidence.limitations: These lung trials used pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. Trial treatment limits and research scan schedules are not automatic NCCP prescribing rules.

chapters.title: Your lung cancer and treatment aim
chapters.intro: First confirm which lung setting applies to you.

items.title: Metastatic treatment
items.text: Metastatic means the cancer has spread. First-line means the first medicine treatment for this stage. Here, pembrolizumab alone is offered for suitable cancers with a high PD-L1 result and without EGFR or ALK alterations. The aim is usually control, symptom relief and more time.

items.title: After surgery
items.text: Adjuvant means treatment after surgery to reduce the chance of cancer returning. This pathway follows complete resection and platinum chemotherapy for cancer at high risk of recurrence. It does not use the same high PD-L1 requirement as the metastatic pathway.

items.title: Your alternatives
items.text: Ask which other treatments, clinical trials, surveillance or symptom-focused care fit your exact cancer and health. Supportive care can help during either pathway.

chapters.title: How pembrolizumab works
chapters.intro: This is an immunotherapy medicine.

items.title: Helping immune cells recognise cancer
items.text: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.

items.title: Why healthy organs can be affected
items.text: The immune system can also attack healthy tissues. Lung, bowel, liver, kidney, skin, gland, heart and nerve inflammation can range from mild to serious. Some hormone changes need long-term replacement.

items.title: A pause is a safety decision
items.text: Your team may delay a dose, treat side effects or stop pembrolizumab. The usual response to immune toxicity is to hold or stop treatment, not to give a smaller dose.

items.title: Before starting
items.text: Your team checks the cancer diagnosis, treatment aim and relevant tumour tests. Blood count, kidney/liver, glucose and thyroid tests provide a baseline. Discuss existing illnesses, medicines, pregnancy and breastfeeding.

chapters.intro: Keep your team informed about what matters to you.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

items.title: During the drip

rationale.summary: PD-1 blockade restores antitumour T-cell activity. First-line metastatic and post-resection adjuvant NSCLC have separate populations, treatment goals and evidence; the shared protocol does not make their eligibility interchangeable.
rationale.setting: Lung cancer only: first-line metastatic NSCLC or adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy
rationale.line: First-line metastatic OR post-resection adjuvant after platinum chemotherapy
factors: Confirm the exact lung indication and treatment aim. Metastatic first-line: validated PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation, stage IV, no prior systemic metastatic treatment, ECOG 0–1.

Adjuvant: complete resection, prior platinum chemotherapy, high recurrence-risk/pathological stage IB–IIIA AJCC7 source criteria, ECOG 0–1; confirm reimbursement/access separately. No metastatic TPS50 eligibility requirement applies.

FBC, renal and liver profiles, glucose and thyroid function. Review autoimmune disease, prior interstitial lung disease, infection, untreated brain metastases, steroid/immunosuppressive use, prior checkpoint treatment, pregnancy/breastfeeding and medicines.
alternatives: Choose among available systemic, targeted, clinical-trial, surveillance and supportive-care options using the precise setting, biomarkers, comorbidity and patient preferences.
limitations: These lung trials used pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. Trial treatment limits and research scan schedules are not automatic NCCP prescribing rules.

KEYNOTE-024: selected untreated metastatic TPS≥50%, no sensitising EGFR/ALK; 66% effective crossover to subsequent PD-1/PD-L1 therapy in the chemotherapy group. Results are not for the adjuvant setting.

KEYNOTE-091 final analysis was presented at ESMO 2026 and reported by the trial sponsor EORTC on 27 October 2026. Chemotherapy-subgroup DFS remained improved; overall survival was not significantly improved at this final, time-triggered analysis. This is conference/sponsor reporting rather than a new full peer-reviewed article. Do not mix these figures with earlier EMA interim snapshots or the trial-wide population.

evidence.trial: KEYNOTE-024 metastatic five-year follow-up; PEARLS/KEYNOTE-091 adjuvant final analysis (ESMO 2026)
evidence.population: KEYNOTE-024: 305 untreated metastatic NSCLC patients, TPS ≥50%, no sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations. KEYNOTE-091: 1,177 completely resected stage IB (tumour ≥4 cm)–IIIA AJCC7 patients; the adjuvant DFS result shown is specifically the 1,010-patient chemotherapy subgroup.
evidence.comparison: Metastatic KEYNOTE-024: pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=154, up to 35 cycles) versus platinum chemotherapy (n=151). Adjuvant KEYNOTE-091 chemotherapy subgroup: pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=506, approximately one year/18 doses) versus placebo (n=504).
evidence.applicability: These lung trials used pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. Trial treatment limits and research scan schedules are not automatic NCCP prescribing rules.

day_groups.title: Your infusion visit

support.title: Sickness medicines
support.text: Pembrolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

support.title: Hormones and steroids
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least four months after the last dose. If pregnancy is possible or occurs, contact your oncology team promptly.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: The adjuvant course lasts up to 12 months. Metastatic treatment continues while helpful and tolerable; a 24-month review may lead to stopping or continuing. Symptoms, response and your preferences can change the plan.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between six-weekly infusions.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

questions.q: Does an abnormal blood test mean pembrolizumab must be stopped permanently?
questions.a: Not by itself. Your team checks whether the change is caused by immune inflammation, another medicine, cancer or another illness. They decide whether to pause treatment, investigate further or stop it. Do not change the treatment plan yourself.

patient.scope_note: This patient suite covers the two lung indications described here. The shared clinical protocol also lists other cancers, which need their own patient information.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be offered
evidence.intro: In a trial of suitable people with metastatic lung cancer and a high PD-L1 result, pembrolizumab helped people live longer than chemotherapy. After surgery and chemotherapy, a separate trial found a lower risk of recurrence or death. Its final long-term analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in overall survival. The aims and evidence differ between these settings.
evidence.interpretation: These results describe groups of people, not what will happen to one person. The metastatic and after-surgery studies answer different questions.
evidence.population: Two separate lung settings: untreated metastatic PD-L1-high NSCLC; and resected NSCLC at high recurrence risk after chemotherapy.
evidence.limitations: The lung trials below used 200 mg every 3 weeks. The 400 mg every 6 weeks schedule is supported by drug-exposure modelling and regulatory bridging; it was not the randomized schedule in those lung trials.

chapters.title: Your lung cancer and treatment aim
chapters.intro: First confirm which lung setting applies to you.

items.title: Metastatic treatment
items.text: Metastatic means the cancer has spread. First-line means the first medicine treatment for this stage. Here, pembrolizumab alone is offered for suitable cancers with a high PD-L1 result and without EGFR or ALK alterations. The aim is usually control, symptom relief and more time.

items.title: After surgery
items.text: Adjuvant means treatment after surgery to reduce the chance of cancer returning. This pathway follows complete resection and platinum chemotherapy for cancer at high risk of recurrence. It does not use the same high PD-L1 requirement as the metastatic pathway.

items.title: Your alternatives
items.text: Ask which other treatments, clinical trials, surveillance or symptom-focused care fit your exact cancer and health. Supportive care can help during either pathway.

chapters.title: How pembrolizumab works
chapters.intro: This is an immunotherapy medicine.

items.title: Helping immune cells recognise cancer
items.text: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.

items.title: Why healthy organs can be affected
items.text: The immune system can also attack healthy tissues. Lung, bowel, liver, kidney, skin, gland, heart and nerve inflammation can range from mild to serious. Some hormone changes need long-term replacement.

items.title: A pause is a safety decision
items.text: Your team may delay a dose, treat side effects or stop pembrolizumab. The usual response to immune toxicity is to hold or stop treatment, not to give a smaller dose.

chapters.title: Your treatment course
chapters.intro: The appointment pattern and total duration are different decisions.

chapters.title: Tests and reviews
chapters.intro: Tell your team about symptoms even when recent blood tests were normal.

items.title: Before starting
items.text: Your team checks the cancer diagnosis, treatment aim and relevant tumour tests. Blood count, kidney/liver, glucose and thyroid tests provide a baseline. Discuss existing illnesses, medicines, pregnancy and breastfeeding.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose before every 6-week cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks, cortisol if indicated, and symptom review throughout and after treatment.

items.title: During a pause or after stopping

chapters.title: Practical support and everyday life
chapters.intro: Keep your team informed about what matters to you.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use the contact plan given by your oncology service.

items.title: Report warning symptoms
items.text: Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

items.title: During the drip
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately if you become itchy, flushed, breathless, dizzy, tight-chested or suddenly unwell.

items.title: Care after treatment ends

rationale.summary: PD-1 blockade restores antitumour T-cell activity. First-line metastatic and post-resection adjuvant NSCLC have separate populations, treatment goals and evidence; the shared protocol does not make their eligibility interchangeable.
rationale.setting: Lung cancer only: first-line metastatic NSCLC or adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy
rationale.line: First-line metastatic OR post-resection adjuvant after platinum chemotherapy
factors: Confirm the exact lung indication and treatment aim. Metastatic first-line: validated PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation, stage IV, no prior systemic metastatic treatment, ECOG 0–1.

Adjuvant: complete resection, prior platinum chemotherapy, high recurrence-risk/pathological stage IB–IIIA AJCC7 source criteria, ECOG 0–1; confirm reimbursement/access separately. No metastatic TPS50 eligibility requirement applies.

FBC, renal and liver profiles, glucose and thyroid function. Review autoimmune disease, prior interstitial lung disease, infection, untreated brain metastases, steroid/immunosuppressive use, prior checkpoint treatment, pregnancy/breastfeeding and medicines.
alternatives: Choose among available systemic, targeted, clinical-trial, surveillance and supportive-care options using the precise setting, biomarkers, comorbidity and patient preferences.
limitations: The lung trials below used 200 mg every 3 weeks. The 400 mg every 6 weeks schedule is supported by drug-exposure modelling and regulatory bridging; it was not the randomized schedule in those lung trials.

evidence.trial: KEYNOTE-024 metastatic five-year follow-up; PEARLS/KEYNOTE-091 adjuvant final analysis (ESMO 2026)
evidence.population: KEYNOTE-024: 305 untreated metastatic NSCLC patients, TPS ≥50%, no sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations. KEYNOTE-091: 1,177 completely resected stage IB (tumour ≥4 cm)–IIIA AJCC7 patients; the adjuvant DFS result shown is specifically the 1,010-patient chemotherapy subgroup.
evidence.comparison: Metastatic KEYNOTE-024: pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=154, up to 35 cycles) versus platinum chemotherapy (n=151). Adjuvant KEYNOTE-091 chemotherapy subgroup: pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=506, approximately one year/18 doses) versus placebo (n=504).

patient.purpose: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.

rationale.setting: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.
rationale.line: Consolidation after definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy in a curative-intent stage III pathway; not metastatic first-line monotherapy.
factors: Confirm NCCP eligibility, PD-L1 testing, performance status, CRT details and recovery.
Balance durable control and survival evidence against post-radiation lung risk, immune adverse events, pre-existing disease and patient preferences.
Agree route, interval, maximum duration, test ownership, emergency contact and access/reimbursement.
alternatives: Individual alternatives, observation or another treatment pathway require multidisciplinary review of stage, biomarkers, CRT recovery, comorbidity and patient preferences; no cross-trial ranking is implied.
limitations: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.
PACIFIC directly studied durvalumab every two weeks after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. This guide uses that interval.

The numerical OS/PFS results below come from the same exploratory five-year update with data cutoff 11 January 2021. They are not mixed with the original co-primary endpoint analyses or presented as individual benefit.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

Controlled hormone-replacement endocrinopathies have a stated exception to the general severe/recurrent immune-event stop rule.

agents.name: Durvalumab
agents.explanation: Durvalumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can reduce the immune system’s ability to attack cancer cells. Removing this signal can help immune cells act against cancer, but the immune system can also inflame healthy organs.
agents.mechanism: Blocks PD-L1 to support immune recognition of cancer
visual: PD-L1 can dampen an immune response
Immune cells can act against cancer cells
risks: Inflammation of the lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys or skin
Thyroid, adrenal, pituitary or blood-sugar problems that may need long-term replacement treatment
Rare serious inflammation of the heart, muscles or nerves
Infusion reactions, fatigue and infections; effects can appear after treatment ends
agents.watch: Report new symptoms early and carry the immunotherapy alert card. Do not wait for the next infusion.

anatomy: Report new or worsening cough, breathlessness or chest pain promptly, including after finishing radiotherapy.
Severe headache, dizziness, confusion, unusual weakness or thirst need prompt assessment; collapse or seizures need emergency help.
Chest pain, palpitations, marked weakness or trouble swallowing can signal serious inflammation; seek urgent help.
Report yellow eyes/skin, dark urine or significant upper abdominal pain; blood tests may detect changes before symptoms.
Report new diarrhoea, blood in stools or significant abdominal pain; do not assume this is ordinary stomach upset.
Report much less urine, swelling or a change in urine; attend kidney blood tests.
Report a spreading rash. Blistering, peeling or mouth/eye sores need urgent assessment.

evidence.intro: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
evidence.population: Unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent platinum chemoradiotherapy, without progression
evidence.interpretation: In PACIFIC, durvalumab reduced cancer worsening and improved overall survival compared with placebo after chemoradiotherapy. The results describe groups of trial participants and do not predict what will happen to one person.

support.title: Immune side effects and the alert card
support.text: Immune side effects may start during treatment or after the last dose. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and tell every treating clinician that you have received durvalumab, even during a treatment break or after finishing.

support.title: Lung symptoms after radiotherapy
support.text: Radiation inflammation, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can cause similar symptoms. Report new or worsening breathing symptoms promptly so the team can assess the cause. Do not assume a new cough is only an old radiotherapy effect.

support.title: Support medicines
support.text: Durvalumab alone has minimal sickness risk and no routine premedication is specified. Use anti-sickness or other medicines only as prescribed. Steroids for an immune reaction are a treatment plan supervised by the team, not routine premedication; do not start, reduce or stop them yourself.

support.title: Hormone replacement and blood tests
support.text: Thyroid, adrenal or diabetes problems may need hormone replacement or insulin, sometimes long term. Keep taking prescribed medicines and attend blood tests even when you feel well. Sudden severe weakness, vomiting, faintness, unusual thirst or drowsiness need urgent advice.

support.title: Pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy plans, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Effective contraception is advised during durvalumab and for at least three months after the last dose. Durvalumab is not recommended during pregnancy. The team must help decide whether breastfeeding or durvalumab should be stopped or avoided, weighing the benefits and risks.

questions.q: Is this more chemotherapy?
questions.a: Durvalumab is an immunotherapy infusion. It follows the completed chemotherapy and radiation course and works by changing immune signalling.

questions.q: How long will I receive it?
questions.a: Durvalumab is infused on Day 1 of each 28-day cycle. The course lasts up to 12 months (13 cycles), and can finish earlier if the cancer progresses or side effects make continuation unsuitable. The first dose should start within 42 days after chemoradiotherapy finishes.

questions.q: Why report a cough after chest radiotherapy?
questions.a: Radiation effects, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can look alike. The team needs to assess new or worsening symptoms rather than assume their cause.

questions.q: Will I need routine steroids before each infusion?
questions.a: No routine premedication is specified for this regimen. Steroids may be prescribed to treat particular immune side effects, with a supervised dose and taper.

questions.q: Can side effects happen after I stop?
questions.a: Immune side effects may start during treatment or after the last dose. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and tell every treating clinician that you have received durvalumab, even during a treatment break or after finishing.

rationale.summary: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
rationale.setting: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.
rationale.line: Consolidation after definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy in a curative-intent stage III pathway; not metastatic first-line monotherapy.
factors: Confirm NCCP eligibility, PD-L1 testing, performance status, CRT details and recovery.
Balance durable control and survival evidence against post-radiation lung risk, immune adverse events, pre-existing disease and patient preferences.
Agree route, interval, maximum duration, test ownership, emergency contact and access/reimbursement.
alternatives: Individual alternatives, observation or another treatment pathway require multidisciplinary review of stage, biomarkers, CRT recovery, comorbidity and patient preferences; no cross-trial ranking is implied.
limitations: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.

PACIFIC studied durvalumab every two weeks. The every-four-week schedule is supported by regulatory drug-exposure bridging; PACIFIC did not directly compare these two schedules or test this fixed dose as its randomised treatment.

For body weight ≤30 kg, NCCP requires 10 mg/kg every two weeks OR 20 mg/kg every four weeks until weight is >30 kg. The clinician must select and prescribe the interval; the fixed-dose card is not an automatic weight-based calculation.

The numerical OS/PFS results below come from the same exploratory five-year update with data cutoff 11 January 2021. They are not mixed with the original co-primary endpoint analyses or presented as individual benefit.
NCCP Table 1 explicitly uses CTCAE 4.03. Confirm the event-specific grade and alternative causes; general interface CTCAE5 aids are not a substitute for this source standard.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

General restart criteria require recovery to grade ≤1, steroid dose ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent and resumption within 12 weeks. Organ-specific permanent-stop rules take precedence. Controlled hormone-replacement endocrinopathies have a stated exception to the general severe/recurrent immune-event stop rule.
No durvalumab dose-reduction ladder is recommended for toxicity. Mild/moderate baseline renal or hepatic impairment requires no dose adjustment; data in severe impairment are limited.

Regular endocrine and organ-function monitoring is required; the NCCP source does not prescribe a routine trastuzumab-style cardiac imaging schedule. New cardiac symptoms require targeted urgent assessment.
Omitted inputs remain unassessed; a reassuring single domain does not authorise treatment. Source reconciliation and software checks are not independent consultant/pharmacy approval.

clinical_notes: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.

PACIFIC studied durvalumab every two weeks. The every-four-week schedule is supported by regulatory drug-exposure bridging; PACIFIC did not directly compare these two schedules or test this fixed dose as its randomised treatment.

For body weight ≤30 kg, NCCP requires 10 mg/kg every two weeks OR 20 mg/kg every four weeks until weight is >30 kg. The clinician must select and prescribe the interval; the fixed-dose card is not an automatic weight-based calculation.

The numerical OS/PFS results below come from the same exploratory five-year update with data cutoff 11 January 2021. They are not mixed with the original co-primary endpoint analyses or presented as individual benefit.
NCCP Table 1 explicitly uses CTCAE 4.03. Confirm the event-specific grade and alternative causes; general interface CTCAE5 aids are not a substitute for this source standard.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

General restart criteria require recovery to grade ≤1, steroid dose ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent and resumption within 12 weeks. Organ-specific permanent-stop rules take precedence. Controlled hormone-replacement endocrinopathies have a stated exception to the general severe/recurrent immune-event stop rule.
No durvalumab dose-reduction ladder is recommended for toxicity. Mild/moderate baseline renal or hepatic impairment requires no dose adjustment; data in severe impairment are limited.

Regular endocrine and organ-function monitoring is required; the NCCP source does not prescribe a routine trastuzumab-style cardiac imaging schedule. New cardiac symptoms require targeted urgent assessment.
Omitted inputs remain unassessed; a reassuring single domain does not authorise treatment. Source reconciliation and software checks are not independent consultant/pharmacy approval.
This date-free journey shows completed concurrent CRT followed sequentially by durvalumab; it does not schedule chemotherapy and durvalumab together.

patient.title: Atezolizumab + carboplatin + etoposide
patient.purpose: To control extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, relieve symptoms and help people live longer. The balance of benefit, side effects and time in treatment should be reviewed with you.

agents.name: Atezolizumab
agents.explanation: Atezolizumab is an antibody against PD-L1, a signal that can reduce an immune cell’s activity. Blocking that signal can help immune cells attack cancer. It works differently from chemotherapy. The same immune activation can inflame healthy organs, so new symptoms need assessment even when they look like ordinary treatment tiredness or a minor infection. IV and SC formulations use different doses but both carry immune risks.
agents.watch: Report new cough, breathlessness, diarrhoea, rash, severe headache, weakness, thirst, frequent urination or chest symptoms promptly. Effects can appear during treatment or after the final dose.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, hormone glands, skin, heart, muscles or nerves
Serious infusion or SC-related reactions
Some effects require prolonged treatment or lasting hormone replacement

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but also affects healthy tissues such as bone marrow. Kidney function is used to calculate its dose. It is given during the four-cycle induction phase and stops before atezolizumab-only maintenance.
agents.watch: Report fever, shivering, unexpected bruising, bleeding or persistent vomiting. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, itching, chest tightness, breathing changes or pain around the drip.
risks: Low blood counts, infection, anaemia and bleeding
Nausea, vomiting and fatigue
Allergic reactions; renal function affects dosing

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA damage can then accumulate and stop cell division. Healthy rapidly renewing tissues can also be affected, explaining low blood counts, hair loss and mouth or bowel problems. Oral absorption differs from IV delivery; the prescribed oral dose must not be inferred from the IV dose.
agents.watch: During an infusion, report dizziness, breathing changes, rash or pain at the drip. At home report fever, mouth ulcers, diarrhoea or poor intake. If capsules are prescribed, follow the exact labelled doses and contact the team about a missed or vomited dose rather than replacing it yourself.
risks: Low blood counts and infection
Hair loss, mouth soreness, nausea and bowel changes
Infusion reactions or low blood pressure during administration
Possible later treatment-related leukaemia; discuss longer-term risks

phases.label: Induction · up to four cycles
phases.detail: Day 1 all three medicines; etoposide also Days 2–3. A cycle is 21 days. Confirm the exact IV/SC/oral route plan.

phases.label: Maintenance · after induction
phases.detail: Chemotherapy stops. Atezolizumab continues every 21 days while appropriate; there is no fixed total number here. Review benefit, symptoms and supportive prescriptions.

timeline.label: Blood counts / infection
timeline.text: Counts may fall between visits · timing varies

timeline.label: Immune effects

day_groups.title: Day 1: treatment and checks
day_groups.body: The team checks symptoms and blood tests, then gives atezolizumab, carboplatin and etoposide during induction. Atezolizumab may be IV or SC. Tell staff immediately if you feel unwell during treatment.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm whether Days 2–3 mean IV visits or oral etoposide at home, and check the anti-sickness plan.

day_groups.title: Days 2–3: etoposide during induction
day_groups.body: You either attend for etoposide drips or take the separately prescribed etoposide capsules twice daily, according to your confirmed plan. Capsules are taken on an empty stomach. Maintenance does not include etoposide.
day_groups.action: Do not switch between the IV and oral schedules or infer capsule amounts. Contact the team about missed or vomited doses.

day_groups.title: After the chemotherapy days
day_groups.body: Sickness, reduced appetite, fatigue or bowel changes may occur. Take the anti-sickness medicines on your written schedule, including later days. The team should check coverage after the last chemotherapy day.
day_groups.action: Ask for advice if vomiting continues or you cannot drink. Report new diarrhoea promptly because immune bowel inflammation is also possible.

day_groups.title: Keep checking how you feel
day_groups.body: Blood counts may fall between visits. The day number does not tell you whether your counts are safe. Hair loss, mouth soreness or fatigue can affect daily life; ask for symptom support.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent contact plan for fever, shivers or sudden illness, including when your temperature is normal.

day_groups.title: Prepare for the next review
day_groups.body: Some symptoms may settle while others persist or appear for the first time. The next dose depends on your review and tests. Around the end of induction, the team discusses whether to move to atezolizumab-only maintenance.
day_groups.action: Bring your symptom record and medicines list. Confirm the next date and which phase and routes are planned.

support.title: Day 1 carboplatin anti-sickness plan
support.text: Carboplatin has a high sickness risk. Your prescription usually includes several anti-sickness medicines with some doses on later days. Follow the written plan even if you initially feel well; contact the team if it is not effective.

support.title: Days 2–3 etoposide and the days afterwards
support.text: The team should account for each chemotherapy day and for two days after the last dose. The later-day plan may overlap the medicines already started on Day 1, so obtain one clear schedule and do not add duplicate doses. Confirm the plan for oral etoposide separately.

support.title: Maintenance support changes
support.text: When only atezolizumab remains, routine chemotherapy anti-sickness steroids and other prophylaxis are not automatically continued. Keep any individual rescue or hormone-replacement plan and the immunotherapy alert card. Do not stop prescribed long-term steroids yourself.

questions.q: What is treatment trying to achieve?
questions.a: Ask how likely this plan is to help control your cancer and symptoms, what alternatives exist, and when you will review benefit.

questions.q: Which routes am I receiving?
questions.a: Confirm IV or SC atezolizumab and IV etoposide on Days 1–3 versus IV Day 1 with oral etoposide twice daily Days 2–3. Ask for a written plan.

questions.q: How long will induction take?
questions.a: Four 21-day cycles occupy about 12 weeks if there are no delays. Chemotherapy then stops; atezolizumab maintenance may continue while appropriate.

questions.q: Who arranges my tests and scans?
questions.a: Confirm blood tests before each cycle, thyroid checks every 3–6 weeks and the consultant’s scan plan. Ask who checks and explains the results.

questions.q: What changes when maintenance starts?
questions.a: Carboplatin and etoposide stop. The visit pattern and anti-sickness plan change, but immune symptom reporting and blood/hormone checks continue.

questions.q: Who do I call outside clinic hours?
questions.a: Keep your oncology emergency number and written temperature/symptom instructions. Do not wait for the next appointment when unwell; show your immunotherapy alert card.
