chapters.title: Understanding this treatment
chapters.intro: A three-medicine induction phase, then atezolizumab-only maintenance.

items.title: Your treatment aim
items.text: To control extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, relieve symptoms and help people live longer. The balance of benefit, side effects and time in treatment should be reviewed with you.

items.title: How the phases fit together
items.text: Induction: atezolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1, with etoposide on Days 1–3, repeated every 21 days for up to four cycles. Maintenance: carboplatin and etoposide stop; atezolizumab alone continues every 21 days while appropriate. The fourth cycle ends about 12 weeks after starting if there are no delays; maintenance has no fixed total duration in this regimen.

items.title: Confirm your route plan
items.text: Confirm your written route plan. Atezolizumab may be a drip (IV) or an injection under the skin of the thigh (SC). Etoposide may be IV on Days 1–3, or IV on Day 1 with prescribed capsules twice daily on Days 2–3. These schedules use different doses; do not change route or convert doses yourself. A separately prescribed four-week IV atezolizumab maintenance plan uses NCCP 00593 and is outside this 21-day calendar.

items.title: Reviewing benefit and choices
items.text: Symptoms, scans and how treatment affects your daily life all matter. Ask when benefit will be reviewed and what would prompt a delay, change or stop. There is no universal scan calendar in this NCCP regimen. You can revisit consent and discuss supportive care at any point.

chapters.title: Before the first treatment
chapters.intro: Use this as a conversation checklist. Your own hospital’s instructions and prescription take priority.

items.title: Tell the team your starting point
items.text: Describe your usual breathing, bowel pattern, energy, skin symptoms and ability to manage daily tasks. Mention autoimmune illness, organ transplant, previous lung inflammation, infections and all regular medicines. Changes are easier to recognise when the team knows what is normal for you. Do not minimise symptoms because you are worried treatment will be delayed.

items.title: Make the first week manageable
items.text: Have the oncology and out-of-hours numbers available, a working thermometer, your medicine schedule and a way to get urgent help. Ask who to ring if you miss a supportive medicine. Plan transport and practical help if needed. Bring your questions and, if you wish, someone you trust to listen and take notes.

items.title: During the infusion visit
items.text: Expect symptom and blood-test review before medicines are released. Chemotherapy is given through agreed venous access; atezolizumab may be a drip or a thigh injection. Tell staff immediately about pain or swelling around the treatment site, itching, flushing, dizziness or breathing changes. Preparation and observation add to the visit time.

chapters.title: What your tests and scans are checking
chapters.intro: Different checks answer different questions: whether treatment is safe today, whether a symptom needs investigation, and whether the cancer is responding.

items.title: Blood counts: three separate jobs
items.text: Neutrophils help fight infection; a low level can make infection dangerous. Haemoglobin carries oxygen; a low level can contribute to tiredness and breathlessness. Platelets help stop bleeding; low levels can cause bruising or bleeding. Feeling well does not prove your counts are normal, and a previous normal result does not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Kidney, liver and hormone checks
items.text: Kidney function helps the team calculate carboplatin and review etoposide dosing. Liver and kidney tests can also reveal immune inflammation or other problems before symptoms develop. Glucose is checked each cycle and thyroid function every three to six weeks. Fatigue, weakness, thirst, dizziness or new headaches may need extra tests; do not assume that they are ordinary treatment effects.

items.title: Scans and the treatment decision
items.text: Your team sets the scan schedule and compares scans with symptoms and examination findings. Stable disease can be a worthwhile result. New symptoms need review even before the next scan. An unusual scan pattern sometimes needs clarification; do not assume that apparent growth is simply an immune response or that feeling worse means treatment is working.

items.title: Why a delay or a change can be appropriate
items.text: A pause may allow recovery or investigation. Chemotherapy doses can sometimes be reduced. Atezolizumab is generally held or stopped for relevant toxicity rather than dose-reduced. Ask which drug is changing and why; stopping one drug does not automatically mean stopping every part of the plan. Long-term treatment decisions belong in a discussion about benefit, risk and what matters to you.

chapters.title: Side effects: what they mean and what to do
chapters.intro: These are selected possibilities, not a prediction or a complete medicine leaflet. You do not need to work out the cause before asking for help.

items.title: Nausea, vomiting and appetite change
items.text: Medicines can stimulate sickness pathways in the gut and brain. Take preventive anti-sickness medicines as prescribed, even when you initially feel well. Smaller meals and frequent sips may be easier. Report poor control early so the plan can be adjusted. Persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or much less urine need prompt advice. Do not wait until you are very dehydrated.

items.title: Fatigue: common, but not always “just treatment”
items.text: Fatigue may reflect treatment, disturbed sleep, reduced intake, anaemia or another illness. Balance rest with manageable movement and prioritise activities that matter to you. A sudden change, severe weakness, dizziness, breathlessness or inability to manage basic tasks needs assessment; hormone problems and other complications can resemble ordinary tiredness. Tell the team how fatigue affects daily life, not just that you feel tired.

items.title: Mouth soreness, ulcers and taste
items.text: Treatment can injure the lining of the mouth. Use a soft toothbrush, gentle mouth care and the rinses recommended by your team. Choose softer foods and avoid foods that sting. Ask for pain relief early. Report ulcers, white patches, painful swallowing or reduced intake; difficulty drinking or fever needs urgent advice. Arrange dental care with the oncology team before procedures.

items.title: Diarrhoea or abdominal pain
items.text: Chemotherapy can upset the bowel, and atezolizumab can cause bowel inflammation. Report new diarrhoea promptly, including stools above your usual pattern, blood, mucus, pain or night-time symptoms. Do not assume that it is ordinary chemotherapy upset. Severe pain, bleeding or dehydration needs urgent assessment.

items.title: Constipation
items.text: Anti-sickness drugs, opioid painkillers, less food and less movement can slow the bowel. Ask about a bowel plan if you are prone to constipation or take opioids. Keep track of your usual pattern. Increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen or inability to pass wind needs prompt assessment rather than simply increasing laxatives.

items.title: Bruising, bleeding or breathlessness
items.text: Chemotherapy may reduce platelets or red cells. Report unexpected bruises, nosebleeds, bleeding gums or increasing breathlessness. Heavy bleeding, black stools with weakness, severe chest pain or severe breathing difficulty need emergency help. Do not start iron or alter blood thinners without review: the cause and treatment need to be established.

items.title: Skin, hair and nerve changes
items.text: Etoposide can cause hair loss, which may affect scalp and body hair. Ask about practical support before it begins. Report a new or spreading rash, tingling, numbness or weakness. Blisters, peeling skin or sores involving eyes or mouth need urgent assessment because immune skin reactions can be serious. Use gentle skin care and ask about suitable sun protection.

chapters.title: Atezolizumab: symptoms that deserve special attention
chapters.intro: Immune treatment can cause inflammation in healthy organs, during treatment or after it ends. Keep your immunotherapy alert card and tell other healthcare professionals you have received atezolizumab.

items.title: Lungs, bowel, liver and kidneys
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling can signal inflammation. These symptoms also have other causes, including infection and cancer. Contact the team promptly for assessment rather than trying to identify the organ or diagnosis yourself.

items.title: Hormones, heart and nervous system
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or changes in vision. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures or major breathing difficulty require emergency care. Some hormone effects need ongoing replacement treatment even after immunotherapy stops.

items.title: Why early reporting matters
items.text: The team may pause treatment and investigate. Some reactions need steroids or other immune-suppressing treatment; others need hormone replacement. These are different from the short planned steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or stop a prescribed course yourself. Carry the treatment name when attending emergency care.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is a plan that fits your life as well as your treatment. Bring practical concerns to the team early.

items.title: Food, fluids and weight
items.text: Aim for enough food and fluid to maintain strength, using foods you tolerate. Tell the team about weight loss, swallowing problems or difficulty shopping or cooking; ask for dietitian support. A fixed fluid target is not right for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney disease. “Anti-cancer” diets, fasting and high-dose supplements are not substitutes for treatment and can create nutritional or interaction problems.

items.title: Movement, work and rest
items.text: Try activity that feels manageable and increase or reduce it according to symptoms. Short walks or simple daily tasks may be more realistic than your usual exercise. Discuss work adjustments and travel plans. Do not drive if dizzy, unusually tired or affected by sedating medicines. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment, not an attempt to push through exercise.

items.title: Infection precautions without isolation
items.text: Wash hands, practise food hygiene and avoid close contact with people who are unwell. Ask about vaccinations and their timing; some vaccines are unsuitable during treatment. You can usually still spend time with family. Keep your urgent contact plan available: precautions reduce risk but do not make fever or sudden illness safe to watch at home.

items.title: Intimacy, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Treatment may harm a developing baby; ask for a written contraception plan covering all three medicines and the period after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment; confirm when it would be safe to restart. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Ask about barrier protection and handling body fluids under your hospital’s advice.

items.title: Emotional support and choices
items.text: It is reasonable to feel worried, angry, uncertain or overloaded. Ask for psycho-oncology, counselling, social work or family support. You can request information in smaller pieces, an interpreter or a written summary. Tell the team what you most want to preserve in daily life. You can revisit treatment decisions and ask for more time or another explanation.

chapters.title: A short treatment dictionary
chapters.intro: Terms you may hear in clinic.

items.title: Cycle · induction · maintenance
items.text: A cycle is a planned treatment-and-interval period. Induction is the initial combination phase. Maintenance is ongoing treatment after that phase; it does not mean side-effect-free treatment.

items.title: Response · stable disease · progression
items.text: Response means the cancer has reduced by the assessment used. Stable disease means it has not changed enough to meet response or progression criteria. Progression means growth or spread meeting the assessment criteria. Your team interprets these alongside how you are feeling.

items.title: Neutropenia · anaemia · thrombocytopenia
items.text: Neutropenia means low infection-fighting neutrophils. Anaemia means low haemoglobin. Thrombocytopenia means low platelets. These are different results with different implications; one normal number does not establish that all treatment risks are low.

items.title: Immune-related · colitis · pneumonitis
items.text: Immune-related effects come from immune activity against healthy tissue. Colitis means inflammation of the colon; pneumonitis means inflammation in the lungs. A symptom alone cannot establish either diagnosis.

chapters.title: Your route and capsule plan
chapters.intro: The NCCP source lists four combinations of routes. Your team must select and prescribe one clearly.

items.title: IV or SC atezolizumab
items.text: The IV formulation runs through a drip; the SC formulation is injected under the skin of the thigh. Their doses differ. The nurse checks the correct formulation and injection site. Both can cause immune and administration reactions; tell staff about pain, swelling, rash, dizziness or breathing changes.

items.title: Etoposide Days 2–3
items.text: The standard IV schedule has a drip on all three days. The oral alternative has IV etoposide on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2–3. Follow the exact capsule label and empty-stomach instructions. Do not calculate a replacement oral dose from a drip dose, split a capsule or double a missed dose. Ask the team what to do after a missed or vomited dose.

items.title: Handling and supply
items.text: Keep capsules in their original labelled packaging, away from children. Follow the pharmacy’s handling and disposal advice; ask what carers should do if a capsule is damaged. Check the full supply and both daily doses before leaving the unit. Do not use remaining capsules for a later cycle unless the team confirms the new prescription.

items.title: Changing phase
items.text: All carboplatin and etoposide finish when induction ends. Atezolizumab-only maintenance in this guide is every three weeks. If your team selects four-week IV maintenance, obtain the separate written schedule; this guide must not be used to convert it.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: In a randomised trial in previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, adding atezolizumab to carboplatin and IV etoposide improved survival and delayed progression on average. This cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.interpretation: In a randomised trial in previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, adding atezolizumab to carboplatin and IV etoposide improved survival and delayed progression on average. This cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.population: Adults with previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer in IMpower133.
evidence.limitations: IMpower133 studied IV atezolizumab with IV etoposide. It did not directly randomise the SC formulation or the Day 2–3 oral etoposide alternative; those are separate NCCP-listed schedules. Trial averages are not an individual prognosis or a comparison with another immunotherapy.

sections.title: Your written formulation plan
sections.text: Confirm your written route plan. Atezolizumab may be a drip (IV) or an injection under the skin of the thigh (SC). Etoposide may be IV on Days 1–3, or IV on Day 1 with prescribed capsules twice daily on Days 2–3. These schedules use different doses; do not change route or convert doses yourself. A separately prescribed four-week IV atezolizumab maintenance plan uses NCCP 00593 and is outside this 21-day calendar.

sections.title: Travel, support and medicines
sections.text: Induction usually involves treatment on three consecutive days or one IV day plus prescribed capsules at home. Ask about transport, work, caring responsibilities and who to call about capsules or symptoms. Carry the immunotherapy alert card.

sections.title: Tests and maintenance
sections.text: FBC, liver, renal and glucose profile before every cycle; thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks. Scans and other disease assessment follow the consultant plan. Continue symptom review during maintenance and after atezolizumab stops because immune effects may be delayed. Confirm which team books each test and who reviews it before treatment.

anatomy: Unusual weakness, dizziness, headache, thirst or frequent urination: report promptly.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment; infection, cancer or clot can look similar.
Chest pain, racing heartbeat or fainting needs urgent assessment.
Report yellow skin/eyes or dark urine; tests may detect changes before symptoms.
Report much less urine, swelling or persistent vomiting; kidney results affect the plan.
New diarrhoea, severe pain, mouth ulcers or difficulty drinking need advice.
Report spreading rash, blisters, weakness, tingling or difficulty with daily tasks.
Fever, shivers, bleeding or suddenly feeling unwell: contact oncology immediately.

chronology_notes.title: About 12 weeks of induction if on schedule
chronology_notes.text: Four 21-day cycles include both treatment days and the interval before the next cycle; delays can extend the course.

chronology_notes.title: No fixed total maintenance length
chronology_notes.text: Atezolizumab continues while the team judges it appropriate, until progression or unacceptable toxicity under this NCCP regimen. The plan is reviewed with you.

chronology_notes.title: Day 2–3 route matters
chronology_notes.text: These days are IV visits or prescribed oral etoposide twice daily. They are not days without treatment during induction.

chronology_notes.title: Checks continue after chemotherapy
chronology_notes.text: Maintenance still requires cycle bloods, thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks and ongoing symptom review. Immune effects may begin after the last atezolizumab dose.

patient.timeline_note: This reference describes a 21-day cycle. Symptoms do not follow a fixed safe/unsafe calendar, and improving symptoms do not prove blood counts have recovered. Your written treatment plan sets dates and route.
patient.safety_note: These materials explain the three-week NCCP00689 regimen and its explicitly prescribed route alternatives. They are educational and cannot establish treatment suitability, calculate doses or replace the team’s written prescription.

rationale.summary: First-line ES-SCLC chemo-immunotherapy: PD-L1 blockade with carboplatin/etoposide induction followed by atezolizumab maintenance.
rationale.why_this_regimen: Combines initial cytotoxic disease control with an immune-mediated contribution established in the IMpower133 randomised comparison.
limitations: IMpower133 studied IV atezolizumab with IV etoposide. It did not directly randomise the SC formulation or the Day 2–3 oral etoposide alternative; those are separate NCCP-listed schedules. Trial averages are not an individual prognosis or a comparison with another immunotherapy.
The NCCP regimen requires consultant initiation, independent prescribing judgment and current local policy. Source reconciliation is not clinical authorisation.

factors: Confirm adult first-line ES-SCLC, ECOG 0–1 and adequate marrow/organ function; review symptoms, medicines and pregnancy possibility. FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, thyroid function, hepatitis B (HBsAg and HBcoreAb) and hepatitis C screening. Measured isotope GFR preferred; otherwise verify a suitable estimate. Record baseline breathing, bowel, skin and endocrine symptoms.
Assess ability to attend the three-day IV schedule or safely follow the explicit oral alternative.
Weigh immune toxicity, comorbidities, anticipated benefit and patient priorities.
alternatives: Discuss other appropriate systemic regimens, clinical trials and symptom-focused supportive care according to suitability, availability and patient preferences.

key_points: Four 21-day induction cycles, then atezolizumab-only maintenance every 21 days.
IV atezolizumab 1200 mg versus SC 1875 mg are explicit alternatives; separate 1680mgIV/28-day maintenance follows NCCP 00593.
IV etoposide 100 mg/m² Days 1–3 versus IV Day 1 then 100 mg/m² PO twice daily Days 2–3; never convert silently.
Immune attribution, named-event grade, recurrence and restart context matter.
Platelets 50–<75 are unassigned in Table 5; etoposide non-dialysis CrCl<10 is unassigned in Table 6.
NCCP gives no atezolizumab dose-reduction scheme; hold or discontinue as specified.

Myocarditis, myositis and myasthenia gravis can overlap. If one is suspected, assess for the other syndromes; apply the most stringent applicable event-specific action. Suspected myocarditis requires withholding and prompt cardiology work-up; diagnosed Grade 2 or higher requires permanent discontinuation.

disease_and_biomarker_context: Adult first-line extensive-stage SCLC; no previous systemic treatment for ES-SCLC.
ECOG 0–1; adequate marrow and organ function. PD-L1 testing was not required for IMpower133 entry and is not an NCCP eligibility requirement here.
key_exclusions_or_cautions: Hypersensitivity to any component; pregnancy/lactation; symptomatic CNS metastases; active clinically significant infection requiring treatment; symptomatic ILD.

Medical condition requiring immunosuppressive systemic corticosteroids (>10 mg prednisolone-equivalent daily, excluding inhaled/topical) or other immunosuppressants. Distinguish the short antiemetic course.
Clinically significant autoimmune disease: caution. Previous anti-PD-1/PD-L1 exposure: review NCCP linked guidance.
Review renal method, obesity/low creatinine and all medicines/interactions.

support_summary: Carboplatin AUC 5 Day 1: NCIS V8 dedicated AUC≥4 antiemetic row, not generic cisplatin HEC.
Account for etoposide Days 2–3 and two days after; reconcile overlapping doses in one prescription. Oral alternative needs an explicit local plan.
Atezolizumab maintenance has minimal emetogenic potential; no routine chemotherapy prophylaxis.
Routine reaction premedication generally not needed; after Grade 1–2 atezolizumab reaction consider antipyretic/antihistamine and close monitoring.
baseline: Confirm adult first-line ES-SCLC, ECOG 0–1 and adequate marrow/organ function; review symptoms, medicines and pregnancy possibility. FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, thyroid function, hepatitis B (HBsAg and HBcoreAb) and hepatitis C screening. Measured isotope GFR preferred; otherwise verify a suitable estimate. Confirm source exclusions, autoimmune history, immunosuppression, prior PD-1/PD-L1, medicine interactions and oral adherence/handling support where relevant.
before_each_cycle: FBC, liver, renal and glucose profile; review symptoms and active phase.
For formula-derived carboplatin dose use creatinine within 48 hours; isotope GFR may be retained only with creatinine≤110% of reference.
Confirm chemo Day 1 count rules and any prior febrile neutropenia; do not presume no-adjustment from a missing value.
ongoing: FBC, liver, renal and glucose profile before every cycle; thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks. Scans and other disease assessment follow the consultant plan. Continue symptom review during maintenance and after atezolizumab stops because immune effects may be delayed.
Thyroid every 3–6 weeks; evaluate other hormones/organ tests as clinically indicated. Source does not prescribe universal cortisol, ACTH or scan intervals.
Immune symptoms may overlap cancer, infection or chemotherapy toxicity; investigate attribution before permanent immune-stop decisions from labs.

For confirmed immune myositis, inability to reduce corticosteroids to 10 mg/day prednisone-equivalent or less within 12 weeks after onset requires permanent discontinuation under the current EMA SmPC; do not infer this from an unrelated steroid prescription.
administration: Day 1 order: atezolizumab, carboplatin, then etoposide. Atezolizumab IV first infusion is 60 minutes, later 30 minutes if tolerated; SC injection takes about 7 minutes. Carboplatin infusion is 30 minutes and etoposide IV is 60 minutes. Total unit time also includes checks, preparation and observation. SC atezolizumab does not remove the chemotherapy drips during induction.

access: Facilities to treat anaphylaxis required for SACT.
SC injection into alternating thighs; ≥2.5 cm from old site and avoid red/bruised/tender/hard skin. Do not give tubing hold-up.
Etoposide IV rate must be respected; monitor infusion reactions and hypotension. Oral capsules on empty stomach; no self-conversion.

evidence.population: 403 adults with previously untreated extensive-stage SCLC, randomised 201 to atezolizumab and 202 to placebo; trial regimen used IV atezolizumab 1200 mg with carboplatin AUC 5 and IV etoposide 100 mg/m² Days 1–3.
evidence.comparison: Atezolizumab versus placebo added to four 21-day carboplatin/etoposide cycles, followed by the assigned atezolizumab/placebo maintenance.
evidence.applicability: IMpower133 studied IV atezolizumab with IV etoposide. It did not directly randomise the SC formulation or the Day 2–3 oral etoposide alternative; those are separate NCCP-listed schedules. Trial averages are not an individual prognosis or a comparison with another immunotherapy.

endpoints.metric: Overall survival
endpoints.result_text: Updated median OS 12.3 versus 10.3 months; HR 0.76 (95%CI 0.60–0.95), descriptive P=.0154.
endpoints.interpretation: Intention-to-treat survival comparison; a difference between medians is not an expected individual life extension.
endpoints.analysis_status: Published 2021 updated analysis; median OS follow-up 22.9 months. Original co-primary OS test was significant at the 2018 interim analysis; updated P value is descriptive.

sources.label: Liu et al. IMpower133 updated OS (2021)

endpoints.metric: Progression-free survival
endpoints.result_text: Primary median PFS 5.2 versus 4.3 months; HR 0.77 (95%CI 0.62–0.96), P=.02.
endpoints.interpretation: Investigator-assessed progression or death in the intention-to-treat population; distinct from overall survival.
endpoints.analysis_status: 2018 primary publication; median follow-up 13.9 months. This endpoint is not presented as a new 2026 or updated-OS analysis.

sources.label: Horn et al. IMpower133 primary analysis (2018)

endpoints.metric: Five-year overall survival (exploratory atezolizumab arm)
endpoints.result_text: Five-year OS 12% (95% CI 7–17) in the reported IMpower133/IMbrella A atezolizumab cohort.
endpoints.interpretation: No long-term control-arm data were available; this does not estimate a five-year comparative benefit or an individual prognosis.
endpoints.analysis_status: 2024 exploratory publication; cutoff 16 March 2023; median follow-up 59.4 months. Eighteen of 26 eligible patients rolled over into IMbrella A; selection and incomplete long-term comparator follow-up limit interpretation.

evidence.qualitative_result: In a randomised trial in previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, adding atezolizumab to carboplatin and IV etoposide improved survival and delayed progression on average. This cannot predict one person’s benefit.
limitations: IMpower133 studied IV atezolizumab with IV etoposide. It did not directly randomise the SC formulation or the Day 2–3 oral etoposide alternative; those are separate NCCP-listed schedules. Trial averages are not an individual prognosis or a comparison with another immunotherapy.
No cross-trial ranking against serplulimab or other immunotherapy.
Trial selection and follow-up differ from an individual’s health and care; the results are not a personal prediction.
NCCP alternative formulations are not separately randomised arms of IMpower133.
The 2024 IMbrella A extension is exploratory with selective rollover and no long-term control-arm data; its five-year result must not be presented as a randomised five-year comparison.

evidence.harms: Discuss chemotherapy myelosuppression, infection, bleeding, nausea, hair loss and treatment burden; atezolizumab adds potentially serious immune organ toxicity that may be delayed or persistent, and administration reactions. Do not substitute trial average efficacy for an individual benefit/risk discussion.

milestones.title: Phase change
milestones.when: After up to four induction cycles
milestones.why: Chemotherapy ends; immune treatment may continue
milestones.clinical: Induction: atezolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1, with etoposide on Days 1–3, repeated every 21 days for up to four cycles. Maintenance: carboplatin and etoposide stop; atezolizumab alone continues every 21 days while appropriate. The fourth cycle ends about 12 weeks after starting if there are no delays; maintenance has no fixed total duration in this regimen.
milestones.action: Confirm atezolizumab schedule and revise anti-sickness medicines without stopping required hormone replacement.

medicines.note: NCIS low-risk row lists metoclopramide 10 mg orally three times daily as needed; account for any already scheduled doses and clinical suitability.

additional_support: NCIS multi-day principle: match prophylaxis to the drugs on each treatment day and continue appropriate cover for two days after.
